a202.text: A caterpillar! One day, it will become a butterfly. Is the caterpillar a nymph, like the young grasshopper?

a301a.text: A little moth is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

a301b.text: Moths rest in the daytime. Look on the walls, and under the leaves!

a301r.text: You against the Buddies! Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

h501.text: Are you ready? Three! Two! One! Go!

a501.text: Round one! Is the caterpillar a nymph? Show me your fingers!

a503.text: One! It is a young insect that munches leaves, just like the grasshopper nymph. So it must be a nymph!

a504.text: Two. A nymph looks like a small adult. But this caterpillar looks nothing like a butterfly.

a505.text: Two! A butterfly has big wings. This caterpillar is just a long, green tube that eats!

a601.text: The answer is two: no, it is not a nymph! Two fingers? One finger up!

a701m.text: Then what is it? It is long and soft, and it wriggles. Is it a worm?

a702.text: Look closer. Count the legs at the front. Then look at the little stumps at the back.

a703p.text: One, two, three pairs of pointed legs at the front. That is six legs, so it is an insect!

a704.text: Like all insects, caterpillars have six legs.

a705.text: The stumps at the back are not real legs. They are called prolegs.

a706b.text: Prolegs are pretend legs with tiny hooks. The hooks grip the twig, so the caterpillar can hold on and crawl along!

a708.text: Prolegs are false legs that help the caterpillars to move.

a801.text: Be a butterfly egg! Shrink down. Quietly.

a802.text: You are a tiny round egg, stuck on a lime leaf. Days go by, and you hatch. You are a little caterpillar!

a803.text: You munch the leaf, and munch, and munch. Your skin gets tight, so you moult, and you grow bigger.

a804.text: One day, you stop eating. You hang very still from a stem.

a805.text: Your skin splits one last time. Underneath, there is a hard case. You are a pupa!

a901.text: The butterfly larva is also called a caterpillar.

a902m.text: So the caterpillar is the butterfly's larva. A larva is the young, and it looks nothing like the adult!

a903.text: The larva eats a lot and moults many times as it grows.

a1001p.text: Now it does not move, and it does not eat. So nothing is happening in there. It is just resting!

a1002.text: Something is not right. If you can spot it, cross your arms. Hold on!

a1004b.text: It does not eat, but it is alive and very busy. Inside its case, it is changing into a butterfly!

a1005.text: This stage is called the pupa.

a1101.text: Look closer. On the outside, the pupa hardly moves. But inside the pupal case, the body is changing.

a1102.text: It does not eat. It continues to develop into an adult in the pupal case.

a1103m.text: So the pupa is busy, like a cake in the oven. You cannot see it change, but it is changing inside!

a1105.text: Then the pupal case splits, and out comes the adult: a butterfly!

a1106b.text: Its wings are all crumpled, like my bedsheet in the morning. Now they are spreading out flat!

a1201.text: The butterfly has four stages in its life cycle. The stages are the egg, the larva, the pupa and the adult.

a1203.text: Some animals have four stages in their life cycles. The young of these animals do not look like the adult.

a1301.text: Show me your score hand! More than one finger? You beat the Buddies. Two fingers? High five!

a1302.text: Did you spot the moth? It was on the side of the lime plant's pot!

a1303.text: Here is a fun fact! Many moth caterpillars spin a silk cocoon, and become a pupa inside it. The silk for silk clothes comes from a moth's cocoon!

h860.text: Let's read today's key words together! Ready?

a1401b.text: Look in this old pail of rainwater! Tiny things are wriggling up and down. What are they?
